schedule.hook: "This is an internal tool, security doesn't matter"
schedule.payoff: Internal tools get compromised. Attackers target the weakest link.
The types ARE the documentation. Define them first.
Working code that's unreadable, insecure, or architecturally wrong creates debt that compounds.
Working code that nobody maintains accumulates security debt and complexity. Maintenance cost grows silently.
Confidence correlates poorly with correctness on novel problems. Moments of certainty are exactly when blind spots hide.

schedule.hook: "I'll commit when the feature is done"
schedule.payoff: One giant commit is impossible to review, debug, or revert. Commit each slice.
If you can't write the user's desired outcome in one sentence right now, the ask isn't clear. Run Step 1 before deciding.
Performance debt compounds. Fix obvious anti-patterns now, defer micro-optimizations.

schedule.hook: "It looks right in my mental model"
schedule.payoff: Runtime behavior regularly differs from what code suggests. Verify with actual browser state.

schedule.hook: "It's working, no need to touch it"
schedule.payoff: Working code that's hard to read will be hard to fix when it breaks. Simplifying now saves time on every future change.
"After" becomes "after the first incident", which is the most expensive moment to discover you're blind. Instrument as you build.

schedule.hook: "This is simple, I don't need a spec"
schedule.payoff: Simple tasks don't need *long* specs, but they still need acceptance criteria. A two-line spec is fine.

schedule.hook: "I'll write tests after the code works"
schedule.payoff: You won't. And tests written after the fact test implementation, not behavior.

schedule.hook: "I'll test it all at the end"
schedule.payoff: Bugs compound. A bug in Slice 1 makes Slices 2-5 wrong. Test each slice.
Confidence is not evidence. Training data contains outdated patterns that look correct but break against current versions. Verify.
Optimize the pipeline (see CI Optimization below), don't skip it. A 5-minute pipeline prevents hours of debugging.

schedule.hook: "I know what the bug is, I'll just fix it"
schedule.payoff: You might be right 70% of the time. The other 30% costs hours. Reproduce first.
Code shows what. It doesn't show why, what alternatives were rejected, or what constraints apply.
It's a legal requirement in many jurisdictions and an engineering quality standard.

schedule.hook: "It works in staging, it'll work in production"
schedule.payoff: Production has different data, traffic patterns, and edge cases. Monitor after deploy.

schedule.hook: "The agent should figure out the conventions"
schedule.payoff: It can't read your mind. Write a rules file — 10 minutes that saves hours.

schedule.hook: "I'll figure it out as I go"
schedule.payoff: That's how you end up with a tangled mess and rework. 10 minutes of planning saves hours.
Security retrofitting is 10x harder than building it in. Add it now.
You will the moment someone has 100+ items. Add it from the start.

schedule.hook: "I wrote it, so I know it's correct"
schedule.payoff: Authors are blind to their own assumptions. Every change benefits from another set of eyes.
If it's needed later, it can be rebuilt. Keeping unused code "just in case" costs more than rebuilding.
Debugging a wrong commit in production is more expensive. The check is bounded; the bug isn't.
Messages are documentation. Future you (and future agents) will need to understand what changed and why.

schedule.hook: "Asking too many questions wastes their time"
schedule.payoff: Time wasted by 4–6 targeted questions is small. Time wasted by building the wrong thing is enormous, and the user is the one bearing that cost.
Your machine isn't the user's. Profile on representative hardware and networks.
Warnings become errors. Clean consoles catch bugs early.
A 1-line nested ternary is not simpler than a 5-line if/else. Simplicity is about comprehension speed, not line count.
Unstructured noise makes incidents slower, not faster. Three queryable events beat three hundred prose lines.

schedule.hook: "I'll write the spec after I code it"
schedule.payoff: That's documentation, not specification. The spec's value is in forcing clarity *before* code.
Simple code gets complicated. The test documents the expected behavior.

schedule.hook: "It's faster to do it all at once"
schedule.payoff: It *feels* faster until something breaks and you can't find which of 500 changed lines caused it.
Hallucinating an API wastes more. The user debugs for an hour, then discovers the function signature changed. One fetch prevents hours of rework.
Trivial changes break builds. CI is fast for trivial changes anyway.
Verify that assumption. If the test is wrong, fix the test. Don't just skip it.

schedule.hook: "We'll write docs when the API stabilizes"
schedule.payoff: APIs stabilize faster when you document them. The doc is the first test of the design.
Retrofitting responsive design is 3x harder than building it from the start.

schedule.hook: "We don't need feature flags for this"
schedule.payoff: Every feature benefits from a kill switch. Even "simple" changes can break things.

schedule.hook: "I'll just correct it when it goes wrong"
schedule.payoff: Prevention is cheaper than correction. Upfront context prevents drift.
Write them down anyway. Explicit tasks surface hidden dependencies and forgotten edge cases.

schedule.hook: "No one would try to exploit this"
schedule.payoff: Automated scanners will find it. Security by obscurity is not security.

schedule.hook: "PATCH is complicated, let's just use PUT"
schedule.payoff: PUT requires the full object every time. PATCH is what clients actually want.
Later never comes. The review is the quality gate — use it. Require cleanup before merge, not after.
Compare migration cost to ongoing maintenance cost over 2-3 years. Migration is usually cheaper long-term.
Only if unscoped. Constrain the prompt to "issues that would make this fail under the contract."
Squashing destroys the development narrative. Prefer clean incremental commits from the start.

schedule.hook: "I'll figure it out as I build"
schedule.payoff: Switching costs after code exists are 10x what they are now. Discovery during implementation is rework.
If you didn't measure, you don't know. Profile first.
DevTools MCP lets the agent verify now, in the same session, automatically.

schedule.hook: "I'll just quickly simplify this unrelated code too"
schedule.payoff: Unscoped simplification creates noisy diffs and risks regressions in code you didn't intend to change. Stay focused.
Unstructured output can't be filtered, correlated, or alerted on. The structured logger costs five extra minutes once.
A 15-minute spec prevents hours of rework. Waterfall in 15 minutes beats debugging in 15 hours.
Tests slow you down now. They speed you up every time you change the code later.

schedule.hook: "These changes are too small to commit separately"
schedule.payoff: Small commits are free. Large commits hide bugs and make rollbacks painful.

schedule.hook: "The docs won't have what I need"
schedule.payoff: If the docs don't cover it, that's valuable information — the pattern may not be officially recommended.
Flaky tests mask real bugs and waste everyone's time. Fix the flakiness.
